findings.target: internal/httpx/middleware.go:177 (AccessLog), :104 (Recover); internal/httpx/ratelimit.go:151 (RateLimit); internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go:203 (logFailure) — vs plan-v7 R8 work item 1
findings.finding: R8 says "the path is REDACTED from the log" — singular. There are FOUR sites that print r.URL.Path, and the redactor cannot help at any of them: internal/logging/logging.go:71 decides on the attribute KEY, the key here is "path", so it never fires. AccessLog's own doc comment defends the wrong half of the URL: "THE QUERY STRING IS NOT LOGGED … a capability lives in the URL" — but DEC-10 puts the capability in the PATH. The sharpest of the four is the rate-limiter's warn line, because it fires precisely when somebody is enumerating share tokens: the one log line written during an attack is the one that records the capability being attacked. A worker who patches AccessLog only will believe R8's requirement is discharged, and the whole suite will be green.
findings.evidence: Executed against the running stack: `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/l/CAPABILITY7XY` then `docker logs`. Recorded verbatim: {"time":"2026-08-24T02:44:06.974Z","level":"INFO","msg":"request","method":"GET","path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY","status":404,...}. The control in the same run confirms the query-string half works: `GET /v1/logbook?secret=INQUERYSTRING` logged as "path":"/v1/logbook" with the query absent. CLAUDE.md L894-900 names the missing URL redactor as an unbuilt requirement belonging to "the step that adds the route"; plan-v7 R8's file list does not include internal/httpx/middleware.go or internal/httpx/ratelimit.go.
findings.fix: Redact in ClientKey's sibling, not at one call site: add a `httpx.LoggedPath(r)` that rewrites `/l/{anything}` to `/l/[redacted]`, and route ALL FOUR sites through it. Add R8 legs asserting each of the four — the rate-limit line especially — and a mutation per site (a fix applied to AccessLog alone must redden three legs). Alternatively make the token a header or a fragment, which removes the class rather than patching it.

findings.target: plan-v7 R3 work item 5 + definition_of_done line 137, vs R8; DEC-51
findings.finding: The capability headers are built in R3 and the capability ROUTE is built in R8, five steps later — and the plan never says how the middleware decides which responses are "capability responses". R3's file list edits internal/httpx/middleware.go; R8's file list does not touch it, and none of R8's work items, legs or mutations mentions the headers at all. GET /l/{token} sits on a different path prefix (`/l/`, not `/v1/`), is unauthenticated, and does not exist when that middleware is written. DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names GET /l/{token} as THE motivating case — plan-v7 wires the fix into the step that does not build it. The consequence is not theoretical: because /l/{token} carries no Authorization header, RFC 9111 §3.5's shared-cache prohibition — the thing silently protecting GET /v1/logbook today — does not apply to it. A 200 with an ETag and no Cache-Control is heuristically cacheable by any intermediary, and after "Stop sharing" a cached envelope keeps handing out live media capabilities for as long as it survives. That unbounds the very window DEC-44 shrank to two minutes.
findings.evidence: Measured on the live server: NO response sets Cache-Control. `curl -i /healthz` → Content-Type, X-Request-Id, Date only. `curl -i -H 'Authorization: Bearer …' /v1/logbook` → Content-Type, X-Request-Id, Date only. internal/httpx/json.go:58 (WriteJSON) sets Content-Type and nothing else; no middleware in serverChain (cmd/api/main.go:293-300) adds a security header. R8's only header-adjacent leg is "a revoked link is 404 byte-identical to an unknown one, headers compared minus X-Request-Id" — which asserts sameness, not presence, and would pass with both headers absent from both answers.
findings.fix: Move the header decision into R8 as well as R3, and make it route-scoped rather than path-prefix-scoped: a `httpx.NoStore()` middleware applied from the route table (a seventh Route field, or the same `!Auth` derivation the limiter uses). Add an R8 leg asserting Cache-Control: no-store, private AND Referrer-Policy: no-referrer are present on the 200 from /l/{token}, with a mutation that drops each. Assert them on POST /v1/media/mint in R3 as DEC-51 also requires.

findings.target: plan-v7 R3 work item 4 + migrations/0001_init.up.sql:119 (media_objects_content_type_present_ck); DEC-51
findings.finding: A three-part chain, and all three parts are missing from plan-v7 at once. (1) The content-type allowlist is referenced in three places and ENUMERATED IN NONE — `image/jpeg` → 0 occurrences in the plan, `heic` → 0; the step titled "the content-type allowlist as a schema constraint" defers the actual list to the worker, and DEC-51's `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$` did not survive from v6. (2) `response-content-disposition: attachment` on the presigned GET → 0 occurrences. (3) `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` was correctly STRUCK by V4-SF3, because S3's response-header override set is closed and no presigned GET can produce it. So plan-v7 has kept the removal of the fallback defence and dropped the primary defence. The shipped schema already accepts the payload: migration 0001's own comment marks its check as "THE WEAKEST CHECK IN THIS FILE" and states that `content_type = 'text/html; <script>'` is accepted. An object stored as text/html is SERVED AS HTML FROM THE BUCKET ORIGIN, at a URL the public share envelope embeds — stored XSS on the storage origin, reachable by anyone holding a share link.
findings.evidence: migrations/0001_init.up.sql:119: `CONSTRAINT media_objects_content_type_present_ck CHECK (content_type <> '')` — the only constraint on the column; lines 95-101 of the same file document the hole in terms. plan-v7 grep counts: `image/jpeg` 0, `heic` 0, `content-disposition` 0, `contentTypeRe` 0. DEC-51 (docs/go-backend-plan-v6.json) states the defence literally: "THE DEFENCE IS THE DISPOSITION PLUS THE ^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$ ALLOWLIST, and the residual is named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered."
findings.fix: Enumerate the list in R3's step text, not in the worker's head — `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$`, in Go for the 422 and as a schema IN-list in migration 0003 (the plan's acceptance check for the schema half is already written and correct). Restore `response-content-disposition: attachment` on every presigned GET, with a leg. Carry V4-SF3's nosniff reasoning forward in a comment so the next worker does not re-litigate it.

findings.target: plan-v7 R2 work item 2 / R3 work item 1 / definition_of_done line 137; DEC-51
findings.finding: The checksum ban is excellent and the size bound is not. DEC-51 required `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT "so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping" — plan-v7 has 0 occurrences of `content-length` and 0 of `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES`, and no config variable for the bound exists. What replaced it is an API-side 422 before signing plus a HEAD on commit. Neither binds the holder of the URL: the 422 happens before the capability is minted, and the HEAD-on-commit only refuses to MARK the object committed — the bytes are already in the bucket. Nothing in these eight steps reclaims them: the media sweep is explicitly out_of_scope ("A media sweep SCHEDULER, and in these eight steps the sweep itself"). So one legitimately-minted upload URL is an unbounded, unreclaimed write. Note the asymmetry is invisible from the DoD, which lists the checksum grep and the byteSize bound in the same breath as though both were enforced by the same mechanism.
findings.evidence: R2 work item 2 (plan-v7:374) states the checksum requirement in full and the DoD backs it with a grep that CAN fail: `grep -rn 'PresignedPutObject\|\.Presign(' internal/media/` returns nothing, plus a real-MinIO 4xx leg. The parallel size requirement has no grep, no MinIO leg, and no number: the only text is "byteSize over the bound is 422 BEFORE anything is signed" (R3 legs) and "a byteSize over the bound" (DoD line 137). "The bound" is never given a value anywhere in the 147 KB plan.
findings.fix: Sign the length too. minio-go's PresignHeader (or PostPolicy for the browser case) carries `Content-Length` into the signature; add MEDIA_MAX_BYTES to internal/config with the other seven, and add a leg mirroring the checksum one — a PUT of more bytes than were signed must be refused BY THE BUCKET, and store.Stat must return an error afterwards. Extend the DoD grep to cover it so the two halves fail the same way.

findings.target: plan-v7 R8 work item 6 and its leg; DEC-10
findings.finding: The indistinguishability requirement lost its stronger half in transit. v6's DEC-10 reads: "'Never existed' and 'revoked' are the SAME 404 WITH THE SAME WORK DONE, so nothing confirms a guessed token was once real." plan-v7 R8 carries only "byte-identical", and its leg compares bodies and headers minus X-Request-Id. `constant-time` appears 0 times in the plan. A handler that returns early on "no row" but resolves the trip, checks the three share flags and mints media URLs for a REVOKED row is byte-identical on the wire and still a clean timing oracle for "this token was once real" — which is the exact property DEC-67's revoke-then-insert history design makes worth attacking. This is a revocation oracle and not a guessing oracle: guessing is bounded by 31^12 ≈ 7.9e17 and is not the concern.
findings.evidence: R8 leg (plan-v7:502): "a revoked link is 404 byte-identical to an unknown one, headers compared minus X-Request-Id"; mutation: "answer 410 for a revoked link". Both are body/status assertions. The precedent for doing this properly already exists in this codebase and is the strongest thing in it — internal/auth/service.go:155-175's eagerly-computed dummyHash, whose leg counts Verify calls rather than timing them. R8 has no equivalent.
findings.fix: Copy the sign-in pattern: resolve the token, and on a miss OR a revocation do the same work before answering — or, more cheaply, make the lookup itself the only branch (select the row regardless of revoked_at, then decide). Add R8's missing leg in the shape the auth one already has: count the store calls on both paths and assert they are equal, rather than timing them.

findings.finding: Rate limiting is either/or, not additive: `if route.Auth { handler = authed(handler) } else { handler = limited(handler) }`. Every authenticated route therefore has NO rate limit whatsoever, now and after all eighteen unbuilt routes land. Against a thirty-day untuned TTL with no revocation surface until R5's DELETE /v1/auth/session, a stolen token buys unlimited whole-log reads and unlimited writes — including R6's DELETE /v1/places/{id}?photos=delete and R5's cascading DELETE /v1/trips/{id}. There is also no "sign out everywhere": R5's revocation is for "this token" only.
findings.evidence: Measured on the live stack: the auth routes 429 after their burst (`401 401 401 401 429 429 …` across 14 requests), while 60 concurrent authenticated-route requests draw no limiter at all. CLAUDE.md L2632-2640 states DefaultSessionTTL is 30 days and "UNTUNED, in the same sense DEC-08's parameters are: nothing has measured it against anything", and L2784: "DefaultSessionTTL has no leg about its VALUE at all."
findings.fix: Make the two middlewares compose rather than alternate — `handler = limited(authed(handler))` — with a second limiter keyed on traveller id (available on the context after RequireTraveller) at a much higher ceiling. Separately: add "revoke all sessions for this traveller" alongside R5's single-token revoke, since a stolen token is precisely the case where you do not know which row to delete.

findings.finding: The code asked for a change that the plan explicitly declines, without arguing it. routes.go:17-18 states: "The day an unauthenticated route arrives that is not a credential attempt, this becomes a sixth field rather than a derivation." R8's GET /l/{token} IS that day, and OE-10 rules "The rate-limited set is already DERIVED from !Auth and stays that way." Two consequences the plan never states. (a) The public read inherits AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN — 10/min by default — which is a CREDENTIAL budget, and is wrong for a share page that fetches an envelope plus a batch media mint. (b) It shares one bucket instance with register and sign-in, keyed on RemoteAddr. Behind the deferred Caddy that bucket is one bucket for the whole internet, so a single person browsing a shared trip exhausts the quota and locks everybody out of signing in — an availability coupling between a public surface and the credential surface, created by a derivation nobody re-examined. R8's only leg is the clause "the public read is rate-limited": no number, and no mutation in R8's list covering it.
findings.evidence: internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go:86 constructs ONE `limited` from ONE `deps.AuthLimit`. deploy/docker-compose.yml: `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN: ${AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN:-10}`. internal/httpx/ratelimit.go:14-20 states the proxy problem in terms and defers it; plan-v7 entry_state confirms it is "STILL TRUE AT THE END OF THESE EIGHT STEPS" and next_slice names it first, "in front of an unauthenticated Argon2 surface costing 64 MiB per attempt AND a public share read". CLAUDE.md L2786-2791 adds that nothing asserts the limiter is per-address at all, because every leg arrives from loopback.
findings.fix: Take the sixth field the code asked for: a `Limit` field on Route with its own ceiling, and a second Limiter instance for the public read so the two budgets cannot exhaust each other. Give R8's leg a number and a mutation. If Caddy is still deferred, say in R8's text that the public read's limit is unenforceable behind a proxy until ClientKey learns X-Forwarded-For — it is the same sentence ratelimit.go already carries.

findings.target: docs/plan-v7.json base.inputs; decisions DEC-76, DEC-77, DEC-78
findings.finding: The plan certifies a hash for the overriding rulings file that does not match the file, never read the last three rulings, and then reused all three of their ids for unrelated decisions. This has a direct privacy consequence rather than only a process one: plan-v7's R5 cites "DEC-77" for stopSharing's explicit reset of the three share flags to true/true/false — and its own test comment says "Removing the reset is a privacy leak, not a tidiness issue — the next link hands out exact pins without anybody having turned that on." A worker who resolves "DEC-77" against the authoritative rulings file finds a decision about capturing two PNGs, and can implement the wrong thing entirely while believing they followed the ruling. The plan's own mechanical gate structurally cannot see this: its uniqueness invariant covers decisions/deferred_decisions/deletions/open_rulings/steps, and the rulings file is not in that list — check-plan.py reports 0 failures.
findings.evidence: Computed directly: rulings-v3-pending.json is 30 rulings, DEC-43..DEC-78, 39,569 bytes, sha256 4c3ab78c75df01e14bd0f08d2a66eca94dab84397f064ea2f651a778280ce1ef. plan-v7 base.inputs claims "the 27 human rulings, DEC-43..75", size 36556, sha256 2c524528e83ec2a1c21e5f7252f5f1ea4abd04368bdf54def9f63d8e93536414, status "READ IN FULL". A scripted id intersection prints three collisions: DEC-76 (plan: capture two sample photographs / ruling: client bumps logbookFormatVersion to 2), DEC-77 (plan: share flag defaults move to migration 0002 / ruling: capture the two fixture PNGs), DEC-78 (plan: make seed is cmd/seed / ruling: the compose service is `postgres`; media before seed).
findings.fix: Re-read the rulings file, re-stamp size and hash, renumber the plan's three decisions to DEC-79..81, and add the rulings file to check-plan.py's uniqueness set so the gate can see the next one. Note that DEC-76 and DEC-78 also already close three of the six open_rulings the plan raises as blockers.

findings.finding: /healthz is unauthenticated, unrate-limited by design ("a liveness probe is not part of the API"), and performs a database PingContext on every call against a pool of DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS=8. It is the one route an unauthenticated caller can use to consume connection-pool capacity without limit.
findings.evidence: Measured: 60 concurrent `curl /healthz` returned 60 × 200 and zero 429s. deploy/docker-compose.yml sets DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS default 8. The detail-suppression half is correct and worth keeping — CLAUDE.md L836-845 records the measured leak it prevents (a pgx error naming hosts, ports and database names).
findings.fix: Loopback-bound today, so this is a note rather than an action. Before anything is published beyond loopback, either put /healthz behind the proxy's own ACL or give it a separate high-ceiling limiter; do not fold it into the auth bucket.
findings.exploitability: reachable now, but both published ports are loopback-bound (verified with lsof), so it needs a deployment change to matter

findings.finding: The deny list names two exact paths — `deploy/.env` and `.env` — and no patterns. `COPY . .` puts everything else in the tree into the build stage and the build cache. A `deploy/.env.local`, `.env.production`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa` or a `secrets/` directory is not covered. This matters more from R2 onward than it does today, because R2 is the step that introduces S3 credentials to this project.
findings.evidence: The file is well-reasoned about the case it closes — the canary measurement is recorded in CLAUDE.md L1288-1297 (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD=hunter2-vs1fixes-canary` recovered from `/src/deploy/.env` in the build stage, and absent after the fix). But the fix was written to the shape of the file that leaked, not to the class.
findings.fix: Add `.env.*`, `!.env.example`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa*`, `secrets/`, `.netrc`, `.aws/`. Keep the existing lines. Cheap, and it is the class rather than the instance.
findings.exploitability: theoretical now; reachable when built (R2 brings S3 credentials)

findings.finding: Three deployment items, all correct for a loopback developer stack and all wrong the moment anything is published: POSTGRES_PASSWORD defaults to the literal `travellog`; DATABASE_URL carries `sslmode=disable`; and the api service sets no `read_only: true`, `cap_drop: [ALL]` or `security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]`. The last is the least urgent because stage 2 is already scratch with a numeric non-root user and no shell — there is very little left to escalate to.
findings.evidence: Read from deploy/docker-compose.yml. Both published ports verified loopback-bound: `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` shows 127.0.0.1:8080 and 127.0.0.1:5434 only.
findings.fix: Leave as-is for the personal build. Add the three to the same checklist that carries the iOS manifest flags — the tier CLAUDE.md calls "guarded by nothing but a human with a device" — so they are read before anything is published beyond loopback.

findings.finding: `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` is present on exactly the responses nobody chose it for and absent from every response the app writes deliberately. The mux's rewritten 404/405 carry it because stdlib `http.Error` set it before envelopeWriter took over; every WriteJSON response — /healthz 200, the 401s, GET /v1/logbook 200 — does not. Low risk on its own (every body is application/json), but it is an inconsistency that will be re-found and re-argued, and the argument is already settled elsewhere: V4-SF3 struck nosniff for presigned GETs because S3 cannot produce it, which is a different reason from "we did not set it here".
findings.evidence: Measured: `GET /v1/nope` → 404 with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; `GET /v1/logbook` (401) and `GET /healthz` (200) → no such header. internal/httpx/json.go:58 sets Content-Type and nothing else.
findings.fix: One line in WriteJSON, or one small `httpx.SecurityHeaders()` middleware in serverChain carrying nosniff for everything and no-store/no-referrer for the capability set (which also gives finding 2 somewhere to land). Record the V4-SF3 reasoning beside it so the bucket case is not re-litigated.

findings.finding: Params.check enforces floors only — there is no upper bound on Memory. A stored PHC encoding with `m=4194304` would have Verify allocate 4 GiB inside a gate slot, and the gate counts slots rather than bytes, so the ceiling the gate exists to provide is not a memory ceiling in that case. Only this build's own Hash writes these rows today, so it needs write access to the database, which is why this is minor rather than major. It is worth a floor-and-ceiling pair anyway because DEC-21's deferred tuning is exactly the moment somebody edits these numbers by hand.
findings.evidence: internal/auth/hasher.go:111-127 — five branches, all of the form `< minimum`. The file's own comment is precise about why the floors exist ("they exist to refuse a panic, not to enforce a policy") and correctly does not claim to bound cost. The gate's arithmetic assumes a fixed 64 MiB: internal/auth/gate.go:6-8, "thirty-two simultaneous logins is 2 GiB".
findings.fix: Add `case p.Memory > maxMemory` (say 1 GiB) and `case p.Time > maxTime` to check(), with the same comment style. It also makes the gate's memory arithmetic true rather than conventional.

verified_correct: NO SIGN-IN ENUMERATION ORACLE, in message or in time — tested, not read. 24 samples across three rate-limit windows against the live stack: known address + wrong passphrase vs unknown address, both 401, medians 24.0ms and 23.5ms, ranges overlapping completely (0.022-0.066 both sides, the high end being first-request warmup on both). The eagerly-computed dummyHash at internal/auth/service.go:168-175 works, and deriving it from DefaultParams rather than writing it as a literal is the detail that keeps it working after DEC-21's tuning.

The rate limiter engages on the credential routes: measured 429 after the burst was spent, `401 401 401 401 429 429 …`. Token bucket, min-ceiling on refill (ratelimit.go:89) so an idle hour does not buy an hour of burst, and prune-when-full is genuinely tuning-free because a full bucket and an absent bucket are the same thing.

The Argon2 concurrency cap REJECTS and never queues — non-blocking select with a default (gate.go:48-55), no timeout to tune because there is no wait. Both Hash and Verify are capped, which is the half that matters (sign-in is the route reachable without creating anything). Every slot returned with defer. Measured ceiling as configured: ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT=2 × 64 MiB = 128 MiB; container RSS 144.4 MiB, consistent.

An unauthenticated caller cannot reach the Argon2 memory ceiling through header abuse: a 40 KB Authorization header answered 401 with no KDF work, because HashToken refuses on decoded length (token.go:63) before hashing. The length check is not redundant with ConstantTimeCompare's own — SameHash's own guard (token.go:78) closes the measured nil-authenticates-against-nil hole.

Session tokens: 32 bytes crypto/rand, base64url on the wire, SHA-256 of the RAW bytes stored as bytea, constant-time compared with an explicit length guard. Authenticate answers ONE sentinel for malformed, unheld, expired, revoked and hash-mismatch (service.go:80-85), so a holder of a stolen token cannot learn which kind of stolen it is.

The request body ceiling is enforced: a 2 MiB register body answered 413, via http.MaxBytesReader at MaxBodyBytes = 1 MiB. Trailing content is refused (the second Decode expecting io.EOF), so two documents in one body cannot report two successful writes.

Query strings are NOT logged — verified by control in the same run as finding 1: `?secret=INQUERYSTRING` does not appear in the access log. The mechanism is right; only the half of the URL it covers is wrong.

SQL is fully parameterised. Every statement in internal/postgres is a const string with $n placeholders; the only Sprintf reaching SQL is in test helpers. logbook_store.go:448's Sprintf builds an InvalidFieldError.Why, and Why never reaches the wire — writeLogbookFailure passes only .Field.

The error body leaks nothing about resource existence and reflects no user input: measured `{"code":"invalid_field","field":"email"}` and `…"field":"passphrase"}` — `field` is drawn from a fixed set of constants, not echoed. The twelve-code vocabulary is closed by three independent mechanisms, and the file is right that typing alone does not do it (an untyped string constant converts implicitly).

No CORS headers are emitted at all — an OPTIONS preflight is answered 405 with no Access-Control-* — so no browser origin can read this API cross-origin. Combined with a cookieless bearer scheme, there is no CSRF surface. TRACE is answered 405, not reflected.

The container is right: stage 2 is scratch, USER 65532:65532 numeric (correct — `USER nonroot` cannot resolve without /etc/passwd), CA bundle copied explicitly, no shell, health probe via the binary's own flag. All three compensations have standing Docker legs with recorded mutation output, despite three separate 'guarded by nothing' lists in CLAUDE.md still naming them — those lists are stale, and the CA bundle / tzdata / numeric USER are in fact guarded.
Both published ports are loopback-bound, verified with lsof rather than read from compose: 127.0.0.1:5434 and 127.0.0.1:8080. Nothing is reachable from the network without an explicit change.

The middleware order is argued correctly and each position is load-bearing: Recover outermost catches panics from the other middlewares, RequestID above AccessLog so the line can be correlated, AccessLog above Timeout so a timed-out request is still logged. An inbound X-Request-Id is deliberately not trusted, which is the right call with no trustworthy proxy in front.

The checksum half of the upload path is the best-specified thing in plan-v7: the PresignedPutObject/Presign ban is stated in the file, backed by a DoD grep that CAN fail, and by a real-MinIO leg asserting both a 4xx AND that store.Stat errors afterwards ('a refused PUT that still wrote something is the same defect wearing a 4xx'). The per-traveller bucket key `<traveller_uuid>/<sha256>` has a cross-tenant leg and a mutation. Keep all of it exactly as written.

stopSharing resetting all three share flags EXPLICITLY to true/true/false, in the same transaction as the revoke, with an inline failing test — correct, and correctly identified in the plan as a privacy leak rather than tidiness. DEC-67's revoke-then-insert with a partial unique index preserves revocation history, which is what makes the revoked-vs-unknown answer possible at all.
questions_for_human: The public presign TTL has no number. DEC-47 makes S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC 'THE HONEST REVOCATION WINDOW' that D3's and H1's copy must be written against, and plan-v7 says only 'longer' than the private ~2 minutes. It is the single number that decides how long 'Stop sharing' is a lie. What is it? (Note R2's only TTL leg compares the two values to each other, so a handler in R8 that reaches for the private one would redden nothing — worth a leg either way.)

DEC-10 stores the share token in plaintext. Session tokens are hashed, with a whole argued section explaining why the hash is of the raw bytes. There is no parallel argument for share tokens anywhere in CLAUDE.md or in plan-v7 — the plaintext decision is referenced once, in the security-lens trigger, and never re-examined in a step. Given finding 1 puts the same token into the access log, and a DB dump now holds live capabilities in the clear, is plaintext still the ruling? (Hashing costs the revocation-history design nothing: store sha256(token) and keep the revoked_at row.)

The content-type allowlist: is it DEC-51's `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$`, or something else? It is referenced in three places and enumerated in none, and the schema constraint that would enforce it cannot be written until somebody says the list out loud.

POST /v1/auth/register is public and answers 409 on a duplicate — a deliberate, well-argued enumeration surface. Under single-user registration that is nearly harmless, but the route is also the way a stranger gets an authenticated account on a deployed instance. Should registration close after the first traveller, or gate on an env-supplied invite? This is one line and it removes the whole question.
unverifiable: Everything in R2, R3 and R8 — the presigner, the media routes and the public share read — has no code. All findings against them are read from plan-v7 and the rulings, not from behaviour. In particular I could not verify that minio-go's PresignHeader actually signs what R2 needs it to, that MinIO refuses a mismatched checksum, or that the go-directive measurement DEC-43 asks for still holds against the real repository rather than the throwaway module.

Behaviour behind a proxy. Caddy is deferred, so there is no X-Forwarded-For path to exercise and no way to demonstrate the one-bucket-for-the-internet failure rather than reason about it. CLAUDE.md L2786-2791 makes the same admission from the other side: nothing asserts the limiter is per-address, because every leg arrives from loopback, so a limiter keyed on a constant would pass the whole suite.
Whether R8's promised path redaction will cover all four print sites, because it is unwritten. Finding 1 is a prediction about a step, backed by a measurement of the four sites that exist now.

Timing behaviour under real load. The 24-sample timing run is enough to rule out a ~60ms Argon2-shaped oracle and is not enough to rule out a sub-millisecond one; the codebase's own answer (count the calls, do not time them) is better than anything I could measure from outside, and it is already applied on sign-in and already missing on R8.

I did not sign in successfully, create any traveller, or write any row — the timing run used wrong passphrases on both branches specifically so that no session was minted. So GET /v1/logbook's 200 response headers were read from internal/httpx/json.go rather than observed; the 401 and /healthz 200 confirm that no middleware adds a header, which is the same code path.
